intro: The SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 exam held on 27 October 2026 comprised three shifts with varying reported difficulty levels. Shift 1 and Shift 2 have full reports, while Shift 3 has a partial review that requires further corroboration. Unofficial figures suggest good attempts ranged from 20–78 in Shift 1 and 65–88 overall in Shift 2, but the SSC normalises scores across shifts. Candidates generally found the Quantitative sections the most challenging across all shifts, with Reasoning and General Awareness showing mixed difficulty.

faqs.q: What was the overall difficulty level of the SSC CGL Tier 1 exam on 27 October 2026?
faqs.a: Based on candidate reports, Shift 1 was described as Easy to Moderate, Shift 2 as Moderate, and Shift 3 as Easy. The overall perception therefore varies by shift, with most candidates finding the exam between Easy and Moderate.

faqs.q: How did the Quantitative sections compare across the shifts on 27 October 2026?
faqs.a: All three shifts identified the Quantitative section as the toughest part of the paper. Shift 1 featured many advanced calculations under a tight 15‑minute limit, Shift 2 was noted as the most challenging with difficulty ranging from easy to very difficult, and Shift 3’s Quantitative questions were reported as ranging from easy to moderate and felt a bit tough.

faqs.q: What information is available for Shift 3 of the 27 October 2026 exam?
faqs.a: Shift 3 has a partial review published. The shift is reported as Easy overall, with Reasoning, General Awareness, and English sections described as easy, while the Quantitative section ranged from easy to moderate. Because the review is limited, further corroboration is needed before drawing firm conclusions.

faqs.q: Are the reported good‑attempt numbers for the 27 October 2026 exam reliable?
faqs.a: The good‑attempt figures for Shift 1 (20–78) and Shift 2 (65–88 overall) are unofficial and based on candidate reports. For Shift 3, good‑attempt numbers were not reliably reported, so no figures are provided. All numbers should be treated as indicative rather than definitive.

faqs.q: How does the SSC handle score normalization for the shifts on 27 October 2026?
faqs.a: The SSC normalises scores across shifts to ensure fairness, meaning that raw scores from each shift are adjusted to a common scale before final ranking. This process mitigates any variation in difficulty between the shifts.
